XII.
A Petition


“‘Then we are to lose Madame la Comtesse, but I hope only for a few
hours,’ I said, with a low bow.

“‘It may be that only, or it may be a few weeks. It was very unlucky
his speaking to me just now as he did. Do you now know me?’

“I assured her I did not.

“‘You shall know me,’ she said, ‘but not at present. We are older and
better friends than, perhaps, you suspect. I cannot yet declare myself.
I shall in three weeks pass your beautiful schloss, about which I have
been making enquiries. I shall then look in upon you for an hour or
two, and renew a friendship which I never think of without a thousand
pleasant recollections. This moment a piece of news has reached me like
a thunderbolt. I must set out now, and travel by a devious route,
nearly a hundred miles, with all the dispatch I can possibly make. My
perplexities multiply. I am only deterred by the compulsory reserve I
practice as to my name from making a very singular request of you. My
poor child has not quite recovered her strength. Her horse fell with
her, at a hunt which she had ridden out to witness, her nerves have not
yet recovered the shock, and our physician says that she must on no
account exert herself for some time to come. We came here, in
consequence, by very easy stages—hardly six leagues a day. I must now
travel day and night, on a mission of life and death—a mission the
critical and momentous nature of which I shall be able to explain to
you when we meet, as I hope we shall, in a few weeks, without the
necessity of any concealment.’

“She went on to make her petition, and it was in the tone of a person
from whom such a request amounted to conferring, rather than seeking a
favor.

This was only in manner, and, as it seemed, quite unconsciously. Than
the terms in which it was expressed, nothing could be more deprecatory.
It was simply that I would consent to take charge of her daughter
during her absence.

“This was, all things considered, a strange, not to say, an audacious
request. She in some sort disarmed me, by stating and admitting
everything that could be urged against it, and throwing herself
entirely upon my chivalry. At the same moment, by a fatality that seems
to have predetermined all that happened, my poor child came to my side,
and, in an undertone, besought me to invite her new friend, Millarca,
to pay us a visit. She had just been sounding her, and thought, if her
mamma would allow her, she would like it extremely.

“At another time I should have told her to wait a little, until, at
least, we knew who they were. But I had not a moment to think in. The
two ladies assailed me together, and I must confess the refined and
beautiful face of the young lady, about which there was something
extremely engaging, as well as the elegance and fire of high birth,
determined me; and, quite overpowered, I submitted, and undertook, too
easily, the care of the young lady, whom her mother called Millarca.

“The Countess beckoned to her daughter, who listened with grave
attention while she told her, in general terms, how suddenly and
peremptorily she had been summoned, and also of the arrangement she had
made for her under my care, adding that I was one of her earliest and
most valued friends.

“I made, of course, such speeches as the case seemed to call for, and
found myself, on reflection, in a position which I did not half like.

“The gentleman in black returned, and very ceremoniously conducted the
lady from the room.

“The demeanor of this gentleman was such as to impress me with the
conviction that the Countess was a lady of very much more importance
than her modest title alone might have led me to assume.

“Her last charge to me was that no attempt was to be made to learn more
about her than I might have already guessed, until her return. Our
distinguished host, whose guest she was, knew her reasons.

“‘But here,’ she said, ‘neither I nor my daughter could safely remain
for more than a day. I removed my mask imprudently for a moment, about
an hour ago, and, too late, I fancied you saw me. So I resolved to seek
an opportunity of talking a little to you. Had I found that you had
seen me, I would have thrown myself on your high sense of honor to keep
my secret some weeks. As it is, I am satisfied that you did not see me;
but if you now suspect, or, on reflection, should suspect, who I am, I
commit myself, in like manner, entirely to your honor. My daughter will
observe the same secrecy, and I well know that you will, from time to
time, remind her, lest she should thoughtlessly disclose it.’

“She whispered a few words to her daughter, kissed her hurriedly twice,
and went away, accompanied by the pale gentleman in black, and
disappeared in the crowd.

“‘In the next room,’ said Millarca, ‘there is a window that looks upon
the hall door. I should like to see the last of mamma, and to kiss my
hand to her.’

“We assented, of course, and accompanied her to the window. We looked
out, and saw a handsome old-fashioned carriage, with a troop of
couriers and footmen. We saw the slim figure of the pale gentleman in
black, as he held a thick velvet cloak, and placed it about her
shoulders and threw the hood over her head. She nodded to him, and just
touched his hand with hers. He bowed low repeatedly as the door closed,
and the carriage began to move.

“‘She is gone,’ said Millarca, with a sigh.

“‘She is gone,’ I repeated to myself, for the first time—in the hurried
moments that had elapsed since my consent—reflecting upon the folly of
my act.

“‘She did not look up,’ said the young lady, plaintively.

“‘The Countess had taken off her mask, perhaps, and did not care to
show her face,’ I said; ‘and she could not know that you were in the
window.’

“She sighed, and looked in my face. She was so beautiful that I
relented. I was sorry I had for a moment repented of my hospitality,
and I determined to make her amends for the unavowed churlishness of my
reception.

“The young lady, replacing her mask, joined my ward in persuading me to
return to the grounds, where the concert was soon to be renewed. We did
so, and walked up and down the terrace that lies under the castle
windows.

Millarca became very intimate with us, and amused us with lively
descriptions and stories of most of the great people whom we saw upon
the terrace. I liked her more and more every minute. Her gossip without
being ill-natured, was extremely diverting to me, who had been so long
out of the great world. I thought what life she would give to our
sometimes lonely evenings at home.

“This ball was not over until the morning sun had almost reached the
horizon. It pleased the Grand Duke to dance till then, so loyal people
could not go away, or think of bed.

“We had just got through a crowded saloon, when my ward asked me what
had become of Millarca. I thought she had been by her side, and she
fancied she was by mine. The fact was, we had lost her.

“All my efforts to find her were vain. I feared that she had mistaken,
in the confusion of a momentary separation from us, other people for
her new friends, and had, possibly, pursued and lost them in the
extensive grounds which were thrown open to us.

“Now, in its full force, I recognized a new folly in my having
undertaken the charge of a young lady without so much as knowing her
name; and fettered as I was by promises, of the reasons for imposing
which I knew nothing, I could not even point my inquiries by saying
that the missing young lady was the daughter of the Countess who had
taken her departure a few hours before.

“Morning broke. It was clear daylight before I gave up my search. It
was not till near two o’clock next day that we heard anything of my
missing charge.

“At about that time a servant knocked at my niece’s door, to say that
he had been earnestly requested by a young lady, who appeared to be in
great distress, to make out where she could find the General Baron
Spielsdorf and the young lady his daughter, in whose charge she had
been left by her mother.

“There could be no doubt, notwithstanding the slight inaccuracy, that
our young friend had turned up; and so she had. Would to heaven we had
lost her!

“She told my poor child a story to account for her having failed to
recover us for so long. Very late, she said, she had got to the
housekeeper’s bedroom in despair of finding us, and had then fallen
into a deep sleep which, long as it was, had hardly sufficed to recruit
her strength after the fatigues of the ball.

“That day Millarca came home with us. I was only too happy, after all,
to have secured so charming a companion for my dear girl.”

"Then we are to lose Madame la Comtesse, though I trust only for a brief interval," I replied, bowing low.

"It may be merely a few hours, or it could stretch to several weeks," she answered. "His sudden address to me was most unfortunate. Do you recognize me?"

"I assure you, I do not," I stated firmly.

"You shall know me," she declared, "but not at this precise moment. We are far older and deeper friends than you likely suspect. I cannot reveal my identity yet. In three weeks' time, I shall pass your magnificent château, regarding which I have already made inquiries. Then I shall drop in for an hour or two to renew a friendship I cherish with countless fond memories. Just now, however, news has struck me like a thunderbolt. I must depart immediately, traveling a circuitous route of nearly a hundred miles with all possible speed. My difficulties multiply daily. Only the strict reserve I maintain concerning my name deters me from making a singular request of you. My poor child has not fully regained her strength. During a hunt she attended, her horse stumbled beneath her; her nerves have not yet recovered from the shock, and our physician insists she must not exert herself for some time. Consequently, we arrived here via very gentle stages—scarcely six leagues per day. Now, I must journey day and night on a mission of life and death—the gravity of which I shall explain to you upon our meeting, hopefully within a few weeks, without further concealment."

She proceeded to lay out her petition, delivered in the tone of someone granting a boon rather than asking for one. Yet, this was merely mannerism, seemingly unconscious. In substance, her plea was profoundly humble: she simply asked that I agree to take charge of her daughter during her absence.

Considering all circumstances, this was a strange, indeed audacious, request. She effectively disarmed my hesitation by acknowledging every argument against it and casting herself entirely upon my chivalry. Simultaneously, fate seemed to conspire; my own ward stepped to my side and, in a whisper, begged me to invite her new acquaintance, Millarca, to visit. Having just tested the waters, the girl believed that if her mother permitted it, she would delight greatly in the company.

Had I possessed a moment's respite, I would have advised patience, waiting at least until we knew their true identities. But there was no time to deliberate. Assailed simultaneously by both women—and compelled by the refined beauty of the young lady, whose face held an irresistible charm, coupled with the evident elegance and fiery spirit of high birth—I succumbed completely. Overwhelmed, I readily accepted the burden of caring for the young woman, whom her mother named Millarca.

The Countess signaled to her daughter, who listened with solemn attention as her mother recounted, in broad strokes, the sudden summons she had received and the arrangements made for her under my guardianship, emphasizing that I was one of her earliest and most cherished friends. Naturally, I offered the appropriate sentiments, only to realize upon reflection that I had placed myself in a position I did not wholly welcome.

The gentleman dressed in black returned, conducting the lady from the room with extreme ceremony. His demeanor impressed upon me the conviction that the Countess possessed an importance far exceeding her modest title suggested. Her final instruction to me was absolute: no attempt was to be made to uncover more about her than I had already surmised until her return. Our distinguished host, her current guest, understood her reasons.

"But here," she whispered, "neither I nor my daughter could safely remain longer than a single day. I removed my mask imprudently a moment ago, about an hour past, and, too late, I feared you saw me. Thus, I resolved to seize this opportunity to speak briefly with you. Had I discovered you had witnessed my face, I would have thrown myself upon your high sense of honor to guard my secret for weeks. Since you apparently did not see me, I am content; yet, should you now suspect, or later reflect and suspect, who I truly am, I entrust myself entirely to your honor. My daughter will adhere to the same secrecy, and I am certain you will, from time to time, remind her lest she thoughtlessly betray it."

She murmured a few words to her daughter, kissed her hurriedly twice, and departed, escorted by the pale gentleman in black, vanishing into the throng.

"In the next room," Millarca said softly, "there is a window overlooking the hall entrance. I wish to bid farewell to my mother and offer her a kiss."

We naturally acquiesced and accompanied her to the glass. Peering outward, we spotted a handsome, old-fashioned carriage surrounded by a retinue of couriers and footmen. There stood the slender figure of the pale gentleman in black, holding a thick velvet cloak. He draped it around her shoulders, pulling the hood over her head. She nodded to him, gently touching his hand with hers. He bowed deeply and repeatedly as the carriage doors closed and the vehicle began to roll away.

"She is gone," Millarca sighed.

"She is gone," I repeated to myself—for the first time, amidst the frantic minutes following my consent—regretting the foolishness of my decision.

"She did not look up," the young lady said, her voice plaintive.

"The Countess may have removed her mask and chosen not to display her face," I reasoned, "and she could not possibly know you were watching from the window."

She sighed again and gazed into my eyes. She was so radiant that my resolve crumbled. I felt remorse for my fleeting moment of coldness toward hospitality and determined to make amends for the unspoken rudeness of my reception.

Replacing her mask, the young lady joined my ward in persuading me to return to the grounds, where the concert was soon to resume. We complied, strolling along the terrace beneath the castle windows. Millarca grew increasingly intimate with us, amusing us with vivid descriptions and tales of many of the great figures we encountered on the terrace. I found her more delightful by the minute. Her gossip, devoid of malice, was exceedingly entertaining to me, who had been so long absent from the grand world. I imagined the vibrant life she would bring to our occasionally solitary evenings at home.

The ball did not conclude until the morning sun had nearly breached the horizon. The Grand Duke danced until then, and loyal subjects dared neither depart nor retire to bed.

As we emerged from a densely packed salon, my ward asked me where Millarca had vanished. I assumed she had remained beside her, and the girl presumed she was by my side. In truth, we had lost her.

Every effort I made to locate her proved futile. I feared she had mistaken others for her new companions in the confusion of a brief separation and, possibly, pursued them into the vast grounds opened to the guests, thereby losing her way.

With growing clarity, I recognized a fresh folly in undertaking the care of a young lady without even knowing her name. Bound by promises regarding the reasons for my acceptance—which I knew nothing of—I could not even direct my inquiries by identifying the missing girl as the daughter of the Countess who had departed mere hours prior.

Daybreak arrived. It was not until nearly two o'clock the following afternoon that we heard word of my missing charge.

About that time, a servant knocked at my niece's door to report that he had been urgently requested by a distressed young lady to ascertain where she might find General Baron Spielsdorf and his daughter, the young woman who had entrusted her care to them.

There could be no doubt, despite minor inaccuracies, that our young friend had reappeared; and so she had. Oh, that we had lost her forever!

She related a tale to explain her failure to locate us for so long. Very late, she claimed, she had reached the housekeeper's bedroom in despair of finding us, only to fall into a deep sleep. Though lengthy, this slumber had barely restored her strength after the exhausting festivities of the ball.

That day, Millarca returned with us. I was only too glad, ultimately, to have secured such a charming companion for my dear girl.
